On Thursday evening, Reddit was named as the newest member of the S&P 500, a move that sent the price of the stock up by around 13%. The company has had a relatively down 2026, with the stock down about 23% year to date, but it remains an interesting company as it attempts to surf a number of trends. At the precise moment that every AI lab in the country is both incredibly deep-pocketed and desperate for novel human-written text upon which to train their models, Reddit’s sitting pretty with 26 billion posts and a wide latitude to license that text. The AI boom is having some negative effects for the company — search traffic is down — but pain now, in the form of reduced Google traffic, in exchange for reward later in the form of licensing deals with the LLMs that intend to replace Google anyway is a pitch that many are buying. Reddit’s exciting for companies that want to advertise because so much of the stuff on the website comes down to what people ought to own. CEO Steve Huffman laid it out plainly in an interview with Yahoo! Finance: "Reddit is so naturally commercial: Forty percent of the conversations people are having organically on Reddit are more or less about what to buy.” The company has made some significant changes to how its homepage works that have meaningfully changed what goes viral on the site, a move that had the effect of diminishing the posts from “karma farmers” and rewarding content from smaller communities. Again, while that’s clearly going to have positive effects on the user experience, it’s also making the site a whole lot more attractive for advertisers. In their most recent earnings call, Reddit executives underscored that they’re thinking a lot about the site’s video experience, and they see that their rivals for user attention — Instagram with its Reels, YouTube with its Shorts, and TikTok with its, well, TikToks — are pulling things off with algorithmic video feeds that Reddit has yet to pull off. Reddit had long maintained a quirky and somewhat idiosyncratic user base (heck, go to a random subreddit and there’s usually a solid chance that the fourth- or fifth-most-upvoted post of all time is still about Ajit Pai) but Reddit doesn’t want a quirky and idiosyncratic user base, they want a billion users, and websites with a billion users ain’t quirky. Stocks pop when companies get into the S&P 500 because that means that millions of retirement accounts and boring index funds must start auto-buying them. Those 401(k)s and set-it-and-forget-it index funds don’t care what time the narwhal bacons, they want ROI, and Reddit won’t have much difficulty deciding whose needs — users or shareholders — come first. For anyone vaguely au fait with the world of online dating, the recent news that Bumble has scrapped one of its central tenets — the women-message-first rule — may have come as a shock, as Bumble begins to look more like many other dating apps in the crowded space. In the statement announcing the shift, Whitney Wolfe Herd, Bumble’s CEO and founder, and a co-founder of Tinder, explained that “While women making the first move was a radical idea, being women-first was never about prescribing just one way to connect.” Per a survey from the dating platform itself back in 2024, 66% of female Bumble users were already saying they preferred men to send the first message. This departure from the core feature that set Bumble apart shows that the company is getting serious about a rather unromantic part of the industry: trying to retain customers. While it could be a good sign for the people who’ve left the app, Bumble hemorrhaging paid users in each of the last seven quarters obviously hasn’t been great for business. body_text: Don’t you hate it when the ATM is down? In Antarctica, that’s a serious problem, given that there’s only one working cash machine on the whole continent, at McMurdo station . It’s the southernmost ATM machine in the world. There is another ATM right next to it, but that one doesn’t work, it’s just there so there’s spare parts in case the working one goes on the fritz. If you’re looking to get your foot in the door in the banking industry by working your way from the bottom up, Wells Fargo sends a technician down once every two years for maintenance and upgrades. Stocks were up on Thursday, with the S&P 500 notching a record close. Big Tech is writing some very big checks for AI. Goldman Sachs estimates global AI infrastructure spending could surpass $1 trillion this year. That bill goes well beyond GPUs, covering the data centers, power systems, and other infrastructure needed to put all that compute to work. As AI clusters get larger, thousands of chips need faster links to move data between them, driving demand for switches, transceivers, lasers and fiber. This earnings season is giving investors an important reminder that orders, sales, and deployments don't necessarily move on the same timetable. Take Cisco : The networking giant booked $9.3 billion of AI infrastructure orders from hyperscalers in fiscal 2026, including $4 billion in the fourth quarter alone according to its earnings report . Cisco had guided to roughly $4 billion of AI infrastructure revenue for fiscal 2026 and now expects that figure to reach $7.5 billion in fiscal 2027. Still, traders heavily focused on a decline in product gross margins, which dropped to 66.3% from 68.4% the previous year, and were not impressed by the revenue forecast. Cerebras Systems can serve as another example. The chipmaker reported $180.1 million in second-quarter revenue in its earnings statement , up 74.3% from a year earlier, but below the $194.23 million analysts expected according to Reuters . Its cloud-services revenue roughly quadrupled to $126 million, while hardware sales fell to $54.1 million from $70.3 million a year earlier. Don’t get me wrong, the AI infrastructure boom is still real and hot. Recent earnings show demand piling up across the AI stack: Coherent saw Datacenter & Communications revenue jump to $1.62 billion last quarter. Applied Optoelectronics reported revenue growth , with data-center revenue surging to $107.7 million. Nebius grew quarterly revenue to $582.3 million, with revenue tied to AI cloud business increased sixfold to $575 million. Corning : Optical Communications sales rose 32% to $2.07 billion. As demand for the AI buildout keeps surging, investors are starting to care more about how quickly the AI orders can be delivered, recognized as revenue, and converted into earnings. For much of the AI boom, proving demand was not hard. Huge capex plans, record orders and swelling backlogs gave investors a reason to bet that years of growth were still ahead. This earnings season suggests the bar for many of these stocks has gotten higher. An order booked today can represent real future business, but it still takes time to manufacture the equipment, complete the deployment and recognize the sale. During that wait, costs can rise, margins can move, and the expectations already embedded in a stock can keep climbing. For investors, that means not every giant AI backlog deserves to be valued the same way. The companies that can convert demand into revenue quickly while protecting margins may be rewarded very differently from those whose order books grow faster than their ability to deliver.
